title: Samarkand's Registan
hookLine: the Timurid square of madrasahs in Uzbekistan

lines: A SUN WITH A HUMAN FACE.
ON THE FRONT OF A SCHOOL.
cards: A tiled gateway, taller than the buildings around it. Across its arch, two great striped cats run, each chasing a white deer. Behind each cat rises a sun, and in the sun is a human face, calm, looking straight out at you.
It is not a palace. It is not a picture gallery. It is the front of a school for studying the Qur'an and Islamic law.
And it stands on one of the well-known squares of Central Asia, in the old Silk Road city of Samarkand, in what is now Uzbekistan. The square has a modest name. Today: Samarkand's Registan.

teach.b: Registan, in Persian, is usually explained as the sandy place. It was an open ground in the middle of Samarkand, where people gathered for markets, announcements and public occasions.

Samarkand was the capital of Timur, a conqueror from Central Asia whose campaigns left terrible destruction across many lands, and who also brought craftsmen from the cities he took to build his capital.

His descendants, the Timurids, ruled after him, and some of them spent their wealth on learning. Around the sandy place, they and later rulers raised madrasahs, schools where students lived and studied.
Ulugh Beg, Timur's grandson, built one of the madrasahs that face the square. Tomorrow's lesson is his.
Later came the Sher-Dor, the one with the cats and the suns, and the Tilya-Kori, whose name speaks of gold, with a mosque inside covered in gilding.
A madrasah is a courtyard ringed with small rooms, where students slept, read, copied and argued, with a teacher's lecture hall and a place to pray.
The Qur'an's first revelation, as tradition tells it, begins with a command to read.

teach.h: READ: IN THE NAME OF THY LORD.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth." And it goes on to speak of the Lord who taught by the pen. And the cats on the Sher-Dor?
Mosques and madrasahs commonly use letters and patterns rather than pictures of living creatures, and some scholars disapproved of such pictures. The Sher-Dor's builders put them right on the gate.
People still argue about what the suns and cats meant.

how: Madrasahs are schools of Islamic learning where students study the Qur'an, hadith and law, traditionally living in rooms around a courtyard; the Registan's madrasahs are now visited as historic monuments.

games.q: you're building a madrasah on the Registan. religious buildings here usually avoid pictures of living creatures. what goes on your gate?
o: cats chasing deer, and suns with human faces.
games.why: the Sher-Dor's builders put cats, deer and faced suns on the gate. people still argue about what they meant.

practice: Look at a photo of the Registan, or of the Sher-Dor gate with its cats and suns, or picture an empty patch of sand in a city with schools rising on its sides.
Find the gate, the domes, the doors to the students' rooms, and think of one thing you're learning right now, however small. If you pray, you can ask for understanding.
